title: Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation in Administrative Action

content.overview: Legitimate expectation protects a person who has been led to expect a particular procedure or benefit from a public authority by reason of an express promise, a regular past practice, or a published policy. The doctrine primarily secures procedural fairness before a departure from the expectation. Substantive protection is more limited and remains subject to statutory power and overriding public interest.
content.glance: Identify the representation, practice or policy that generated the expectation; test whether the expectation is legitimate; determine whether procedural fairness required a hearing before departure; and assess any claim to substantive protection against statutory limits and public interest.
content.study:
Core rule: where a public authority has, by promise, settled practice or published policy, generated an expectation that a person will be treated in a particular way, fairness may require that the authority not depart from that course without affording an opportunity to be heard.

Sources of expectation: An expectation may arise from (1) an express assurance or promise, (2) a regular and consistent past practice, or (3) a published policy or circular. The expectation must be clear, reasonable and induced by the authority's own conduct.

Procedural protection: The ordinary remedy is procedural. Before departing from the expected course, the authority should give the affected person notice and a chance to make representations. This links legitimate expectation to the broader requirement of audi alteram partem.

Substantive protection: Indian courts have been cautious about converting legitimate expectation into a rigid substantive right to a particular outcome. Any substantive claim remains subject to the statutory power of the authority and to overriding public interest. The doctrine cannot compel an authority to act ultra vires or to freeze policy permanently.

Limits: No legitimate expectation arises from an unlawful promise, from a mere hope, or from conduct that is too vague to generate a reasonable expectation. Change of policy is not by itself unlawful; the question is whether fairness required a hearing or other safeguard before the change affected the claimant.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in the Constitution and the specific statute creating the administrative power. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of legitimate-expectation doctrine; evidence provisions apply only when proof issues arise.

sections.heading: Meaning and Purpose
sections.body: Legitimate expectation is a fairness doctrine that protects reliance on a public authority's promise, practice or published policy. Its primary purpose is to ensure that a person is not taken by surprise by a sudden departure from an expected course without an opportunity to be heard.

sections.heading: How an Expectation Arises
sections.body: Identify a clear representation, a consistent past practice, or a published policy attributable to the authority. The expectation must be reasonable in the circumstances. Vague hopes, unlawful promises, or unilateral assumptions by the claimant do not generate a protected expectation.

sections.heading: Procedural Protection
sections.body: Where a legitimate expectation is established, fairness ordinarily requires notice and an opportunity to make representations before the authority departs from the expected course. This procedural protection is the core of the doctrine in most cases.

sections.heading: Substantive Claims and Public Interest
sections.body: Substantive protection — a claim to the expected benefit itself — is more limited. Courts examine whether the authority has statutory power to deliver the expected outcome and whether overriding public interest justifies departure. The doctrine cannot force an ultra vires act or freeze policy indefinitely.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Relief may include a direction to afford a hearing before departure, quashing of a decision taken without fairness, or remittal for a lawful decision. Substantive relief is exceptional and must fit within the statutory framework.

examples.title: Departure from published policy without hearing
examples.body: A department publishes criteria for processing a class of applications and then rejects an application under different, unannounced criteria without giving the applicant a chance to respond. The issue is whether a legitimate expectation of policy-based treatment arose and whether procedural fairness was breached.

examples.title: Change of policy in public interest
examples.body: An authority that had followed a long-standing practice announces a new policy for the future and offers affected persons a chance to make representations. The issue is whether the change is lawful once procedural fairness is observed and public interest is shown.

examples.title: Unlawful promise
examples.body: An officer promises a benefit that the governing statute does not authorise. The claimant relies on the promise. The analysis must recognise that an ultra vires assurance cannot generate a legitimate expectation that compels an unlawful act.

hypotheticals.question: Does every change of administrative policy violate legitimate expectation?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Policy may change. The questions are whether an expectation arose, whether fairness required a hearing before the change affected the claimant, and whether overriding public interest justifies the departure within statutory power.

hypotheticals.question: Can legitimate expectation compel the authority to grant a substantive benefit?
hypotheticals.analysis: Only in limited circumstances. First confirm that the expectation is legitimate and that the authority has power to grant the benefit. Then assess public interest and statutory limits. Procedural protection is the ordinary outcome; substantive relief is exceptional.

distinctions.title: Legitimate expectation vs audi alteram partem
distinctions.left: Legitimate expectation is triggered by the authority's own promise, practice or policy.
distinctions.right: Audi alteram partem is the general fair-hearing requirement before adverse administrative action.

rows.left: Representation, practice or published policy generating reliance.
rows.right: Adverse decision affecting rights or interests, subject to context.

rows.left: Often supplies the reason why a hearing is required before departure.
rows.right: Broader natural-justice principle applicable even without a prior promise.

distinctions.title: Legitimate expectation vs proportionality
distinctions.left: Legitimate expectation protects reliance on representation or practice.
distinctions.right: Proportionality tests whether means are suitable, necessary and not excessive relative to an aim.

rows.left: Fairness of departing from an expected course.
rows.right: Balance between administrative aim and burden on the affected person.

rows.left: Source of expectation → procedural hearing → limited substantive claim.

misconceptions.trap: Any past practice permanently freezes policy.
misconceptions.correction: Policy may change; the doctrine primarily requires fairness before departure, not permanent substantive entitlement.

misconceptions.trap: An unlawful promise creates an enforceable legitimate expectation.
misconceptions.correction: An ultra vires assurance cannot compel the authority to act outside its statutory power.

misconceptions.trap: BSA provisions create the doctrine of legitimate expectation.
misconceptions.correction: The doctrine arises from administrative-law fairness principles; evidence law is relevant only to evidentiary questions.

cases.name: Union of India v Hindustan Development Corporation
cases.facts: The case concerned claims based on expectations arising from governmental conduct in a commercial and administrative setting.
cases.issue: What is the nature and limit of legitimate expectation in public law?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Legitimate expectation may arise from representation, promise or consistent past practice, but it does not automatically create a substantive enforceable right and remains subject to public interest and lawful policy.
cases.holding: The Court clarified the doctrine's scope and limits on the facts before it.
cases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on the contours of legitimate expectation.

cases.name: Food Corporation of India v M/s Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries
cases.facts: A highest tenderer challenged non-acceptance of its bid and invoked legitimate expectation.
cases.issue: Does legitimate expectation require automatic acceptance of a tender?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Public authorities must act fairly and non-arbitrarily, but legitimate expectation does not confer an automatic right to acceptance of a commercial bid.
cases.holding: The Court rejected an absolute entitlement while requiring fair dealing.
cases.relevance: Authority on fairness, tender decisions and the limits of legitimate expectation.

cases.name: Punjab Communications Ltd v Union of India
cases.facts: A policy change was challenged on the basis of an expectation arising from prior governmental practice.
cases.issue: What is the distinction between procedural and substantive legitimate expectation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The doctrine may protect procedural expectations and, in appropriate cases, substantive expectations, but policy may change for overriding public interest and lawful reasons.
cases.holding: The Court explained the procedural/substantive distinction and limits.
cases.relevance: Authority on procedural versus substantive legitimate expectation and public-interest limitations.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a legitimate-expectation challenge be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the promise, practice or policy said to generate the expectation. II. Test whether the expectation is clear, reasonable and legitimate. III. Determine whether procedural fairness required a hearing before departure. IV. If substantive relief is claimed, test statutory power and overriding public interest. V. Identify the appropriate remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on legitimate expectation contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out the representation, practice or policy and the reliance placed on it; establish legitimacy of the expectation; identify the procedural defect if any; address public-interest and ultra vires limits on substantive claims; and seek only the relief supported by the governing law and record.

keyTakeaways: Expectation arises from promise, practice or policy — not from mere hope.
Procedural protection is the ordinary core of the doctrine.
Substantive relief is exceptional and cannot compel ultra vires action.
Policy change is lawful if fairness and public-interest limits are respected.
